10. Concepts as categories

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-10-harmonise.Rmd
book-10-harmonise.Rmd

What you will learn

Use translated concept answers, distinguish recodes from column renames, and harmonise two different site vocabularies.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses omop.questionnaire_vocab, then the two questionnaire sites.

Start this chapter

Log in first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.questionnaire_vocab", server = "site")$conns

The connection is ready; conns identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

Chapter 4 identifies Education question (900001), Fever question (900002), Secondary education (900101), University education (900102), Yes (900301) and No (900302). The later discovery table in this chapter adds the concepts needed for ordering and classification.

Translation follows the value type

A concept-valued answer is a category, not a quantity to average. With the recipe API, the declared value column supplies that type. Your variable name does not need the suffix _concept_id.

education <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))

The event selects the education question; the reducer reads its last coded answer. Selecting the question concept as the value would answer a different question.

categories <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(categories, out = c(people = "D_categories"), conns = conns)

Translation is the default. The data values become labelled factors on the server.

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_categories$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_categories$education
#>  Secondary education University education                   NA
#>                   12                   12                   24

The latest education answers are Secondary education for 12 people and University education for 12, with 24 missing. The concept IDs used in the definition are vocabulary identifiers; they do not appear as numeric answers in this table.

Recode answers to yes and no

An explicit label map changes categories by concept identity. It does not search for text in each site’s database.

First inspect the default wording:

fever_default <- omop_variable(event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))
fever_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(fever = fever_default))
recipe_execute(fever_recipe, out = "D_fever_default", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_fever_default$fever",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_fever_default$fever
#> Yes  No  NA
#>  12  12  24

The default labels are No and Yes, with 12 people each and 24 missing. Now give those same concepts the study’s lower-case wording:

fever <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"),
  labels = c("900301" = "yes", "900302" = "no"))

Only the declared answer concepts receive those labels. A missing answer stays missing; absence of a record is not a clinical “no”.

answers <- omop_recipe(variables = list(fever = fever),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(answers, out = c(people = "D_category_answers"), conns = conns)
recode_table_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_category_answers$fever", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
recode_table_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_category_answers$fever
#> yes  no
#>  12  12

There are still 12 “no” and 12 “yes” answers. Only the wording changed; this call excludes missing answers. ds.omop.table() also shows declared zero levels.

Rename the column separately

A column name identifies the variable; a label names one of its categories. Name an explicit variable in the recipe list, without changing what its answers mean.

renamed <- omop_recipe(variables = list(schooling = education),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(renamed, out = c(people = "D_renamed_categories"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_renamed_categories", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id" "schooling"

The list name supplies the scalar variable name. A concept label map would instead change values inside that column. The visit walkthrough uses a value-preserving mutate alias when adding a new name to an already assigned date column.

ds.omop.table("D_renamed_categories", "schooling", conns = conns)
#> D_renamed_categories$schooling
#>  Secondary education University education
#>                   12                   12

The education categories and counts are unchanged. Next we address differences between sites, where even the vocabulary names can vary.

Rename automatically generated concept columns

Some layouts expand one event into separate columns for each concept. A panel of inpatient/outpatient counts is one example. column_names targets their stable generated keys, not the explicit scalar variable from the previous step.

Inpatient Visit is 9201 and Outpatient Visit is 9202, found in chapter 4. First build the unrenamed panel and read its public codebook:

visit_event <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", c(9201L, 9202L), name = "visits")
visit_population <- omop_population("visitors", index = omop_index(visit_event))
panel_output <- omop_output("panel", rows = "visitors", format = "person_period",
  options = list(sources = list(visit_event), bins = list(width = 30L),
    window = omop_window(0, 29), analyses = "count"))
panel_recipe <- omop_recipe(events = list(visit_event),
  populations = list(visit_population), outputs = panel_output)
panel_result <- recipe_execute(panel_recipe, out = c(panel = "D_original_panel"), conns = conns)
panel_columns <- recipe_codebook(panel_result)[[1]]$columns
panel_columns[c("stable_key", "name")]
stable_key name
row_id row_id
cohort_row_id cohort_row_id
person_id person_id
period_start_days period_start_days
period_end_days period_end_days
days days
visits_9201_count visits_inpatient_visit_count
visits_9202_count visits_outpatient_visit_count

The count columns have stable keys visits_9201_count and visits_9202_count. Use those keys in the rename map:

renamed_panel <- omop_recipe(events = list(visit_event),
  populations = list(visit_population), outputs = panel_output,
  column_names = c(visits_9201_count = "admissions", visits_9202_count = "outpatient"))

The keys combine the source name, concept identity and analysis. They remain stable when a vocabulary changes its wording; your chosen column names remain readable. An explicit name cannot collide with a protected or another final column.

recipe_execute(renamed_panel, out = c(panel = "D_renamed_panel"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_renamed_panel", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"            "cohort_row_id"     "person_id"         "period_start_days"
#> [5] "period_end_days"   "days"              "admissions"        "outpatient"

The resulting count columns have your declared names. Using column_names with an explicit scalar name such as education would not rename that scalar column.

Find and save the category identities

For the next examples, omop.questionnaire_vocab includes a small synthetic classification catalogue. Its teaching ATC and ICD-10 entries illustrate the hierarchy structure; they are not clinical mappings to reuse in a study. Search the catalogue before choosing an order or a rollup.

catalogue <- ds.omop.concept.search(NULL, standard_only = FALSE, limit = 100,
  conns = conns)$pooled
classification <- catalogue[catalogue$vocabulary_id %in% c("ATC", "ICD10", "Language") |
  catalogue$concept_id %in% c(900101L, 900102L, 900103L, 900201L, 900202L, 950001L), ]
classification[c("concept_id", "concept_name", "vocabulary_id", "concept_class_id")]
concept_id concept_name vocabulary_id concept_class_id
900101 Secondary education Questionnaire Questionnaire
900102 University education Questionnaire Questionnaire
900201 Myocardial infarction Questionnaire Questionnaire
900202 Pneumonia Questionnaire Questionnaire
950001 Questionnaire study medicine Questionnaire Questionnaire
900103 Primary education Questionnaire Questionnaire
4180186 English language Language Language
960001 Teaching ATC first level ATC ATC 1st
960002 Teaching ATC second level ATC ATC 2nd
960010 Teaching circulatory code ICD10 ICD10 Hierarchy
960011 Teaching respiratory code ICD10 ICD10 Hierarchy
960020 Teaching circulatory chapter ICD10 ICD10 Chapter
960021 Teaching respiratory chapter ICD10 ICD10 Chapter 
ids <- setNames(catalogue$concept_id, catalogue$concept_name)
education_ids <- ids[c("Primary education", "Secondary education", "University education")]
education_keys <- paste0("concept:", education_ids)
education_set <- omop_concept_set(unname(education_ids))
category_file <- "category-concepts.rds"
saveRDS(list(answers = education_set), category_file)

The concept_id column supplies the IDs we select below, including Primary education (900103) and English language (4180186). The question and answer concepts were located in observation in chapter 4. Primary education is declared in this catalogue but is not an observed answer. A complete public category domain can include an unused level.

Put primary, secondary and tertiary in order

Alphabetical order is not educational order. Declare stable concept identities, then give the three levels the short labels used by the study.

education_ordered <- omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(
  levels = education_keys, order = omop_category_order(education_keys), ordered = TRUE))
ordered_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education_ordered),
  labels = setNames(c("primary", "secondary", "tertiary"), education_ids))
ordered_result <- recipe_execute(ordered_recipe, out = "D_ordered", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_ordered", "education", conns = conns)
#> D_ordered$education
#>   primary secondary  tertiary
#>         0        12        12

The table follows primary < secondary < tertiary, with primary = 0, secondary = 12 and tertiary = 12. The 24 missing answers are omitted by ds.omop.table(). The order is chosen by the study, not inferred from frequency. Ordered factors use polynomial contrasts; set ordered = FALSE if your model needs nominal treatment contrasts instead. A treatment reference and display order are separate choices.

Check the actual type of this column.

dsBaseClient::ds.class("D_ordered$education", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "dsomop_category_factor" "ordered"                "factor"

It is an ordered factor, not the integers used internally to store a factor.

Choose labels and language

name displays the concept name. code_name adds its vocabulary code; it does not expose numeric concept IDs as answers. A language declaration requests the vocabulary’s synonyms for that language, falling back to a concept name when none is available. It does not translate free text automatically.

language_id <- ids[["English language"]]
styled <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  code_and_name = omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(label_style = "code_name")),
  local_name = omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(
    language = omop_category_language(language_id)))))
style_result <- recipe_execute(styled, out = "D_styled", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_styled", "local_name", conns = conns)
#> D_styled$local_name
#> Secondary schooling  Tertiary schooling
#>                  12                  12

The teaching vocabulary supplies “Secondary schooling” and “Tertiary schooling” as English synonyms, still with 12 people each. The category identity is unchanged by these labels.

Display the code-and-name variant from the same extraction.

ds.omop.table("D_styled", "code_and_name", conns = conns)
#> D_styled$code_and_name
#> secondary - Secondary education tertiary - University education
#>                              12                              12

The counts remain 12/12; each label now includes its public vocabulary code. Use code or vocabulary_code when that coding context is needed. source_code is refused on this route because source-code disclosure needs a separately admitted policy. Prefer names for an ordinary analysis table.

Keep Missing and Unknown distinct

Missing means there is no usable value; Unknown represents OMOP concept zero, “No matching concept”. It does not mean a respondent answered “Don’t know”. Neither means a recorded “no”. The missing policy can make each an explicit factor level without inventing a clinical answer.

missing_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  education = omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(
    missing = omop_category_missing(na = "level", unknown = "level"))),
  sex = omop_category(omop_variable(name = "sex", table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id"), omop_category_spec(
    missing = omop_category_missing(na = "level", unknown = "level")))))
missing_result <- recipe_execute(missing_recipe, out = "D_missing_categories", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_missing_categories", "education", conns = conns)
#> D_missing_categories$education
#>  Secondary education University education              Missing              Unknown
#>                   12                   12                   24                    0

The 24 missing answers are now visible as Missing, alongside 12 Secondary and 12 University answers. The public Unknown level may have zero count; declaring it does not assert that anyone has an unknown answer. The sex column contains FEMALE and MALE; its declared Missing and Unknown levels remain empty.

Check which declared sex levels are actually observed.

ds.omop.table("D_missing_categories", "sex", conns = conns)
#> D_missing_categories$sex
#>    MALE  FEMALE Missing Unknown
#>      28      20       0       0

There are 20 FEMALE and 28 MALE values. A declared Unknown level does not turn an observed FEMALE or MALE value into an unknown value.

Present a semantic flag as an integer, logical or factor

A binary reducer asks whether an event occurred. It has false/true meaning before presentation, so it can safely become 0/1, FALSE/TRUE or named categories.

has_visit <- omop_variable(event = visit_event, reducer = omop_reduce("binary"))
flags <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  integer_flag = has_visit,
  logical_flag = omop_category(has_visit, omop_category_spec(binary = omop_category_binary("logical"))),
  named_flag = omop_category(has_visit, omop_category_spec(binary = omop_category_binary("factor")))))
flag_result <- recipe_execute(flags, out = "D_flags", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_flags", "named_flag", conns = conns)
#> D_flags$named_flag
#>  no yes
#>  12  36

There are 12 “no” and 36 “yes” values. This “no” means no selected visit in the defined history. It does not mean a negative answer to the fever question. Binary presentation is for semantic flags, not an arbitrary two-level concept column.

Inspect the published types without reading patient rows.

flag_columns <- recipe_codebook(flag_result)[[1]]$columns
flag_columns[c("name", "r_type")]
name r_type
person_id character
integer_flag integer
logical_flag logical
named_flag factor

The three columns represent the same flag as integer, logical and factor values. Their R types tell you which representation a downstream method receives.

Roll up drug classes and cause chapters

A rollup follows vocabulary relationships. ATC levels are classification classes, not a number of ancestor steps. ICD-10 chapters require the source coding relationships; a similar-looking code prefix is insufficient.

drug_id <- ids[["Questionnaire study medicine"]]
ancestors <- ds.omop.concept.ancestors(drug_id, conns = conns)$pooled
ancestors[c("concept_id", "concept_name", "min_levels_of_separation")]
concept_id concept_name min_levels_of_separation
960001 Teaching ATC first level 2
960002 Teaching ATC second level 1

The medicine has two teaching ATC ancestors: 960001 and 960002. The separation counts describe the links; ATC level itself comes from the vocabulary class.

icd_id <- ids[["Teaching circulatory code"]]
links <- rbind(
  ds.omop.concept.relationships(icd_id, relationship_id = "Maps to", conns = conns)$pooled,
  ds.omop.concept.relationships(icd_id, relationship_id = "Is a", conns = conns)$pooled)
links[c("concept_id", "relationship_id", "related_concept_id", "related_concept_name")]
concept_id relationship_id related_concept_id related_concept_name
960010 Maps to 900201 Myocardial infarction
960010 Is a 960020 Teaching circulatory chapter

Teaching circulatory code (960010) maps to Myocardial infarction (900201) and belongs to Teaching circulatory chapter (960020). These are synthetic relationships used only for this lesson.

ds.omop.concept.locate(c(drug_id, ids[["Myocardial infarction"]]),
  scope = "pooled", conns = conns)$pooled
concept_id table_name concept_column n_records n_persons
900201 death cause_concept_id 20 20
950001 drug_exposure drug_concept_id 35 35 
classification_sets <- list(answers = education_set, drug = omop_concept_set(drug_id),
  causes = omop_concept_set(unname(ids[c("Myocardial infarction", "Pneumonia")])))
saveRDS(classification_sets, category_file)

The locator shows banded counts: 35 medicine users means 35–39 and 20 myocardial-infarction records means 20–24. Later category tables release exact counts when permitted; the 24 infarctions are consistent with the band 20.

Now choose the public domain to be classified. Here domain means the declared set of source concepts, not the OMOP domain such as Drug or Condition. omop_category_rows() selects the concept category on each event row; omop_category_reduce() then chooses one category per person using a reducer. Ambiguous targets fail by default; resolve them in the study protocol with explicit priority or multiple membership. Do not resolve ambiguity by inspecting patient frequencies.

drug_value <- omop_category_reduce(
  omop_category_rows(omop_event("drug_exposure", classification_sets$drug), "concept_id"),
  omop_reduce("last_value"))
cause_value <- omop_category_reduce(
  omop_category_rows(omop_event("death"), "concept_id"), omop_reduce("first_value"))
rollups <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  atc_first = omop_category(drug_value, omop_category_spec(rollup =
    omop_category_rollup("atc", level = 1, domain = classification_sets$drug))),
  atc_second = omop_category(drug_value, omop_category_spec(rollup =
    omop_category_rollup("atc", level = 2, domain = classification_sets$drug))),
  chapter = omop_category(cause_value, omop_category_spec(rollup =
    omop_category_rollup("icd10", level = "chapter", vocabulary = "ICD10",
      domain = classification_sets$causes)))))
rollup_result <- recipe_execute(rollups, out = "D_rollups", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_rollups", "chapter", conns = conns)
#> D_rollups$chapter
#> Teaching circulatory chapter Teaching respiratory chapter
#>                           24                           12

There are 24 people in the circulatory chapter and 12 in the respiratory chapter. The 12 people with no cause are omitted from this table. The cause counts are grouped by the synthetic chapter relationships. The underlying person roster is unchanged. Use a validated clinical vocabulary for a real cause-of-death classification.

Compare the two ATC levels in the public codebook.

rollup_columns <- recipe_codebook(rollup_result)[[1]]$columns
data.frame(
  Variable = c("atc_first", "atc_second"),
  Category = vapply(rollup_columns$levels[match(c("atc_first", "atc_second"), rollup_columns$name)],
    function(x) paste(x$labels, collapse = ", "), character(1)))
Variable Category
atc_first Teaching ATC first level
atc_second Teaching ATC second level

The first and second levels have different labels even though the same drug records contribute to both. Neither level is selected by counting observed drugs.

Many categories at one site

DataSHIELD lets a site release the categories it observes only when they are few: at most 40 by default, and fewer than a third of the rows (a person’s repeated value counts once). A site that records 60 different causes of death is above that rule. The servers then declare a public list that holds the observed categories themselves: they climb the vocabulary’s hierarchy only as far as the rule needs and declare the categories under those few groups, or, for a vocabulary without a hierarchy, its whole short list. The recipe needs no change, and every site gets the same levels, including categories nobody has. Dates by month, quarter or week work the same way: every period of the observed years becomes a level.

A longer list, such as a large clinical terminology, is refused with the remedies. Group the codes with omop_category_rollup() or omop_category_recode(), narrow the events with concepts =, or declare the codes you study with omop_concept_levels().

Levels that no site uses show as zero counts in tables, but a pooled model cannot estimate them. Before ds.glm(), make a copy that keeps only the levels that some site uses:

ds.omop.drop_empty_levels("D_rollups", newobj = "D_rollups_model", conns = conns)

Read the codebook of each table

Keep the execution result: it carries the admitted table metadata. Calling recipe_codebook() on it is local and does not query patient rows. Calling it on the recipe instead produces a prospective schema, with unresolved fields marked explicitly.

book <- recipe_codebook(ordered_result)
book[[1]]$columns[c("stable_key", "name", "semantic_type", "r_type")]
stable_key name semantic_type r_type
person_id person_id key character
education education category ordered_factor

The stable key identifies the column before a display rename. Semantic type tells you what a value means; R type tells you how it is represented. Units, category levels, ordering, reference, contrasts and derivation belong with the analysis protocol. None of these fields is a count or a missingness estimate.

Two sites with different wording and different answers

Site2 has no Secondary education answers: all its respondents have University answers. Its newer vocabulary calls concept 900102 “University qualification”. Log in to both sites. In a real federation each site has its own server URL; here both resources are on our Opal:

ds.omop.disconnect(conns = conns)
DSI::datashield.logout(conns)
conns <- ds.omop.login(rep("https://localhost:8443", 2), user = "administrator",
  password = "password",
  server = c("site", "site2"),
  resource = c(site = "omop.questionnaire", site2 = "omop.questionnaire_site2"))$conns

Inspect the vocabulary wording before looking at patient counts:

lookup <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(900102L, conns = conns)
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lookup$per_site), function(site)
  cbind(Site = site, lookup$per_site[[site]][c("concept_id", "concept_name")])))
Site concept_id concept_name
site 900102 University education
site2 900102 University qualification

Both names belong to concept 900102. The ID, not the text, establishes the shared category.

Let the default reconciliation work

Execute the original unlabelled education recipe on both connections:

recipe_execute(categories, out = c(people = "D_default_pair"), conns = conns)
paired_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_default_pair$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
paired_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_default_pair$education
#>      Secondary education University qualification                       NA
#>                       12                       36                       48

The pooled counts are Secondary education = 12, University qualification = 36, and missing = 48. Execution already chooses one category per concept ID and uses the newest vocabulary wording. No label map was needed to combine them.

The same two-site response contains counts for each site. Select the count matrix, leaving out the proportion matrices:

site_counts <- paired_counts$output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
colnames(site_counts) <- names(conns)
site_counts
site site2
Secondary education 12 0
University qualification 12 24
NA 24 24

Site has 12 Secondary and 12 University qualification answers, plus 24 missing. Site2 has Secondary = 0, University qualification = 24 and missing = 24. The joint response includes the zero cell and shared wording. Adding its two columns gives the pooled counts above. These are counts from separate sites; this operation does not link people across sites.

Exercise 1: fix the study’s wording

Keep “University education” as the shared label even when a site has a newer name. Does this change the counts?

Solution

harmonised <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education),
  labels = c("900102" = "University education"),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(harmonised, out = c(people = "D_shared"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_shared$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_shared$education
#>  Secondary education University education                   NA
#>                   12                   36                   48

The counts remain 12 Secondary, 36 University and 48 missing. The explicit map fixes wording; it changes neither the question selected nor the answer IDs.

Exercise 2: combine two answer categories deliberately

Give Secondary and University the same label, “Recorded education”. Predict the pooled count and missing count before executing.

Solution

merged <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education),
  labels = c("900101" = "Recorded education", "900102" = "Recorded education"))
recipe_execute(merged, out = "D_merged_answers", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_merged_answers$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_merged_answers$education
#> Recorded education                 NA
#>                 48                 48

Equal labels merge the two categories: 48 people have Recorded education and 48 remain missing across the two sites. This discards the education-level distinction; shared wording alone cannot establish clinical equivalence.

Exercise 3: change the reducer at both sites

Take the first education answer instead of the last. Does either site’s marginal distribution change?

Solution

first_answers <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))))
recipe_execute(first_answers, out = "D_first_pair", conns = conns)
first_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_first_pair$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
first_site_counts <- first_counts$output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
colnames(first_site_counts) <- names(conns)
first_site_counts
site site2
Secondary education 12 0
University qualification 12 24
NA 24 24

Site remains 12 Secondary, 12 University qualification and 24 missing; site2 remains 0, 24 and 24. Adding the columns again gives pooled totals 12, 36 and 48. At site, opposite individual changes cancel in the margins, as chapter 5 showed. At site2 every recorded answer is University. Equal totals do not prove that the first and last selections identify the same answers.

Recap

Concept values translate by default. Label maps recode answers; column maps rename variables. Execution reconciles categories by concept ID; explicit labels fix study wording. A missing category at one site remains an explicit zero after reconciliation.
